messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Memory
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Threat → Memory
  - Threat → Triggers

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

# Chukwu's Reckoning

Chukwu was nineteen when he came to the clinic, though he carried himself with the careful precision of someone much older. He had moved to the States from Lagos five years prior, the youngest of four, sent by his family to build something better. He'd done well—straight through high school, a job at a mid-size accounting firm downtown, a modest apartment he shared with a roommate. The kind of trajectory that was supposed to feel like victory. But six months ago, everything had fractured in a way that no amount of professional success could repair.

It happened on a Friday evening in March. Chukwu had stayed late at the office to finish a client reconciliation. The building was nearly empty by the time he locked his desk and headed to the parking garage. He'd taken the elevator to the third level and was walking toward his car when he heard the stairwell door open behind him. Two men emerged. He didn't recognize them—construction workers, maybe, or maintenance staff—but something in their gait made him uneasy. He walked faster. One of them called out. When he didn't respond, they followed. What happened next unfolded with a terrible swiftness: a hand grabbing his arm, his body slammed against the concrete, the taste of blood and oil in his mouth as his face scraped the ground, the weight of two bodies holding him down, the sound of his own voice breaking as he tried to call for help. The physical pain was immediate and overwhelming, but it was the violation—the absolute theft of his body's autonomy—that shattered something deeper.

In the months that followed, Chukwu had tried to return to normal. He'd filed a police report that went nowhere. He'd told his roommate nothing, had lied to his parents about why he sounded distant on their weekly calls. But his body had learned something new, something that made every ordinary moment feel laden with danger. Loud voices—a colleague raising their tone in a meeting, a customer shouting over the phone—sent him into a state of raw alarm. His chest would tighten, his breath would shallow, and he would find himself back in that garage, bracing for impact. The shouting itself became a portal: it triggered not just fear but the full sensory rush of the memory—the visual flashes of the concrete floor beneath his face, the taste of blood returning to his mouth, the crushing weight on his back. Each time someone raised their voice near him, the memories came flooding back, and with them, a certainty that danger was imminent.

Being alone with men had become intolerable. At work, he began requesting to handle client calls only with female colleagues present, inventing reasons to avoid one-on-one meetings with his male supervisor. When his roommate's friends came over, Chukwu would lock himself in his bedroom. The presence of an unfamiliar man in ordinary space—in a grocery store, on the street, in any enclosed room—felt like a direct threat. His mind had fused the image of those two men in the garage with every stranger's face, every unexpected male presence a potential harbinger of violence. This hypervigilance fed the memories: the more threatened he felt, the more vividly the images returned. A man stepping into the elevator with him would trigger an intrusive flash of the stairwell door opening, the visual memory so sharp and detailed that he could almost feel the impact again.

Doors themselves had become dangerous. The sound of a door slamming in his apartment building could paralyze him for minutes. The opening of an unfamiliar door—a conference room he'd never entered, a client's office—sent a spike of dread through his body. Doors were how they had found him; doors were how danger announced itself. When a door opened unexpectedly, the memory would surge: not always a complete image, but sometimes just the raw emotional terror of that moment, the full intensity of violation flooding through him without a clear picture attached, as if his body remembered what his mind couldn't quite hold. And when he felt that terror—that disembodied panic—he would find himself hyperalert, searching for threats, certain that something catastrophic was about to happen. His threat system had become a closed loop: the memory amplified the fear, the fear made him search for danger, and every unexpected stimulus seemed to confirm that danger was real.

Unfamiliar places had become impossible. He couldn't assess the exits, couldn't predict where threats might emerge, couldn't trust that he would be safe. His world had contracted to a handful of known spaces—his apartment, his office, the route between them. When his firm asked him to visit a new client site across town, he'd called in sick. When a colleague invited him to a work happy hour at a bar he'd never been to, he'd made an excuse. The avoidance felt necessary, protective, but it was also isolating him in ways he couldn't quite articulate to anyone. He hadn't told his supervisor about the trauma. He hadn't told his parents. He'd simply begun to disappear from the life he'd built, shrinking his world to the spaces where he could feel even remotely in control.

By the time he came to the clinic, Chukwu was exhausted. The nightmares had become less frequent, but the daytime intrusions hadn't stopped. He was calling in sick to work more often. His supervisor had begun asking questions. He was afraid—deeply, bone-level afraid—that if he told anyone the truth, they would see him as damaged, as weak, as no longer the capable young man he'd worked so hard to become. What he wanted most was to feel safe again in his own body, in his own city. What terrified him was that he might never be able to trust the world the way he had before.
